scope: Reviewed authored English directions only. No student data.

records.text: Measure distance and hear a warning. At your already-built walking stick. The micro:bit measures how far away an object is. The website shows that distance in centimetres and plays a warning when the object is 30 centimetres away or closer. Keep the built model on a table. Save your old program first, then follow the guide to add distance messages and test them. Check. A nearby object gives X on the micro:bit, a distance on the website and a warning sound. Keep the existing built sensor connections: Trig P0 and Echo P1. Have the teacher check the powered sensor interface before physical tests. Keep the model on a table. This is a classroom prototype, not tested mobility equipment.

Protect the old program and make a test copy. In Make Code · Home → your team project. The complete program will replace the code in a test copy. A backup keeps the earlier team program available. Open your latest team project and download a backup named WalkingStick_BeforeBluetooth.hex. Return Home and create a new project named WalkingStick_Bluetooth_Test. Check. Your earlier .hex is saved, and the new test project is open. Keep the old team project. For an older saved .hex, use Import → Import File before making its backup. The following pages work in the new test project.

Add Bluetooth before pasting. In the new Make Code test project · Extensions. The supplied program uses Bluetooth instructions. Make Code needs the Bluetooth extension before it can recognize that code. Open Extensions and add the official Bluetooth extension to WalkingStick_Bluetooth_Test. Check. The Bluetooth category appears before you paste any program. If Make Code asks to remove the radio extension, Bluetooth uses its place in this test project. Keep the original project and backup. Ask the teacher to resolve a different conflict or a memory error.

Choose the classroom Bluetooth setting. In Make Code · Project Settings. No Pairing Required lets nearby devices connect for this teacher-supervised demonstration. Chrome still asks which device to use. In the test project, select the teacher-approved No Pairing Required setting before pasting and downloading the program. Check. The Bluetooth extension and checked connection setting are ready. If school policy requires a different mode, have the teacher verify that connection route. Do not guess among nearby boards.

Paste the complete program once. In WalkingStick_Bluetooth_Test · JavaScript view. The complete source already contains the sensor read, decisions and Bluetooth sender. Replacing the test editor once avoids duplicate stacks. Open the complete code below and click Copy code. In Make Code choose JavaScript, select all the editor text and replace it with the copied program. Then choose Blocks. Check. Make Code converts the program to five stacks without errors. Later pages inspect these existing blocks; do not add another copy. Select the text inside the code editor, not the whole browser page. On Windows use Ctrl+A then Ctrl+V; on Mac use Command+A then Command+V. If Bluetooth names are not recognized, check the extension. If conversion fails, compare the complete source and keep the old backup.

Inspect the on start stack. In Blocks · on start. on start runs once. Variables are named boxes: stick status stores a word and B T connected stores true or false. you art service prepares Bluetooth text messages. Compare your on start stack with the real block image. Find trigPin P0, echoPin P1, stick status unknown and Bluetooth uart service. Check. These blocks already came from the pasted program. No near/far decision, you art write or repeating pause is inside on start. Make Code hides default initial values in Blocks: echoTime and distanceCm begin at 0; B T connected begins false. The initial unknown is only the starting word. The forever stack later replaces it using a fresh measurement. you art service prepares sending; you art write line actually sends and belongs in forever.

Inspect the sensor-reading function. In Blocks · function readUltrasonicDistance. A function is a named set of instructions. This one sends a short trigger pulse and returns the length of the Echo pulse in microseconds, not centimetres. Find the separate readUltrasonicDistance function. Follow Trig low, wait 2 microseconds, Trig high, wait 10 microseconds, Trig low, then pulse in on Echo with a 2five hundred0-microsecond timeout. Check. The function uses trigPin P0 and echoPin P1. It returns an echo time; the distance conversion happens later in forever. A microsecond is one millionth of a second. The timeout limits how long pulse in waits; a missing pulse returns 0. The return may contain a grey JavaScript block showing pins.pulseIn(echoPin, PulseValue.High, 2five hundred0). That is expected; keep it unchanged.

Inspect the two Bluetooth events. In Blocks · two separate Bluetooth event stacks. An event runs when a connection changes. These events remember the connection state while the separate forever stack reads the sensor. Find on bluetooth connected with set B T connected to true. Find on bluetooth disconnected with set B T connected to false and set stick status to unknown. Check. Both event stacks match the image. They contain no sensor loop, near/far decision or sender. true means a Bluetooth device is connected; false means it is not. Do not drag these blocks into on start. They already exist in the pasted program.

Check the invalid echo first. In Blocks · forever → first if. forever first calls the sensor function and stores its returned time in echoTime. The first if rejects an echo below 116 or above 23200 microseconds. Find set echoTime to call readUltrasonicDistance. Follow the first if: echoTime < 116 OR echoTime > 23200. Inside it, find distanceCm 0, stick status unknown and show string ?. Check. A missing echo returns 0 and enters unknown. This invalid branch runs before any near/far comparison. < means less than; > means greater than. OR means either condition is enough. The accepted echo interval is about 2–400 centimetres. distanceCm 0 here marks an unusable result; it is not a measured zero-centimetre obstacle. Do not move unknown to the end of a straight stack.

Follow a usable echo to near. In Blocks · first if’s else → distanceCm ≤ 30. The outer else handles accepted echoes. Divide echoTime by 58 to get centimetres, then round to one decimal place. The second if checks whether that rounded distance is at or below 30 centimetres. In the outer else, find set distanceCm to round(echoTime ÷ 58 × 10) ÷ 10. Follow distanceCm ≤ 30 to set stick status near and show icon X. Check. Only an accepted echo can become near. Exactly 30 centimetres belongs to this branch. For example, 1177 microseconds becomes about 20.3 centimetres. Multiply by 10, round to a whole number, then divide by 10 to keep one decimal place. The X is the No icon. Keep these supplied blocks together.

Follow a usable farther echo to far. In Blocks · outer else → inner distance check’s else. The inner else runs only after the echo was accepted and the distance was found to be above 30 centimetres. Find the else paired with distanceCm ≤ 30. Follow set stick status to far and clear screen. Check. far gives a blank micro:bit display. The invalid-echo branch is separate and cannot become far. There are two different else branches. The outer else contains the conversion and whole near/far decision. This inner else contains only far and clear screen. Compare their nesting in the image.

Inspect the sender after the whole decision. In Blocks · bottom of the same forever stack. A Bluetooth message carries the result and the distance together. near,20.3 means the object is near and the sensor estimated 20.3 centimetres. The comma separates the two parts. After the sensor decision, find if B T connected. Inside it, unknown sends only stick status. Its else sends stick status joined to a comma and distanceCm. Find pause five hundred after the whole sending if. Check. Each loop sends one line: near,20.3, far,40 or unknown. unknown sends no pretend zero distance. There are two you art write line blocks in different branches. Only one runs for each reading. Both are inside if B T connected and outside the sensor decision. Write line adds the line ending. The pause runs even when disconnected.

Compare all five stacks before running. In Make Code · whole Blocks workspace. The source, real block images and program on the board must agree. Inspecting the layout catches a missing or misplaced section before transfer. Compare all five stacks with the complete image and source below. Check invalid echo first, conversion in its else, near/far inside that else, and the sender after the whole decision. Check. Your test project matches the pasted P0/P1 program. It contains one sensor function, one forever, one on start and two Bluetooth events. This complete source is the same program you pasted earlier. Copy it again only to replace the whole test editor if repairing it; never append a second program. Conversion to Blocks does not prove the physical sensor or Bluetooth connection works.

Save and run the updated program. In Make Code · Download, then the MICROBIT drive. A numbered file records the exact program being tested. The simulator cannot prove a physical ultrasonic reading or Bluetooth link. Download the next unused numbered .hex, for example WalkingStick_02.hex. Copy it to the MICROBIT drive using the checked U S B data cable. Check. Wait for copying and flashing to finish. Keep the cable connected until the board is running the updated program. Keep the earlier backup. If Make Code shows errors or downloading removes a needed setting, resolve that before testing the model.

Open the sound page. In Chrome · a separate tab. The website is already provided. It plays the warning sent by your micro:bit. Browsers wait for a click before allowing sound. Open Walking-stick sounds and click Enable sound. Check. The page is ready to play a warning; connecting is the next step. Use the checked Chrome laptop and HTTPS site. Keep its tab visible during each test. The labelled demo is only a website demonstration, not a Bluetooth test.

Connect your team’s micro:bit. On Walking-stick sounds. Chrome asks which nearby board to connect. Your program must be running on the board you choose. Click Connect micro:bit and select your team’s identified device. Check. The website receives fresh messages. With a usable echo, it shows the sensor distance in centimetres as well as near or far. If no board appears, check Bluetooth, the uploaded you art program and its connection setting. Use the teacher-checked laptop; Chrome on iPhone or iPad cannot make this Web Bluetooth connection.

Test cardboard at 20 centimetres. At the tabletop model · sound tab visible. This checks the whole path: sensor → program → Bluetooth → website → speaker. Use a ruler, not a guessed distance. Place cardboard 20 centimetres from the sensor’s front face. Compare the website’s sensor distance with the ruler, then check the display and sound. Check. A usable reading near 20 centimetres shows X, near, an estimated distance near 20 centimetres and the warning. The ruler shows where you placed the cardboard; the website shows what the ultrasonic sensor estimated. They may differ. If the number is missing, upload the updated program and reconnect.

Move the same cardboard to 40 centimetres. At the tabletop model · sound tab visible. Keep the object and setup the same while changing the distance. The result must come from a valid new reading. Move the cardboard to 40 centimetres from the sensor face and observe again. Check. A usable reading near 40 centimetres gives a blank display, far and an estimated distance near 40 centimetres. The warning stops. The sound page says Beyond 30 centimetres. That describes the reported measurement, not proof that the surroundings are safe.

Check an unusable sensor reading. With your teacher · sound tab visible. The first if must report unknown for a missing echo or an echo outside the accepted interval. Test this path with the teacher as well as the near and far paths. Have your teacher run a safe missing-echo or out-of-range test for this built model. Check. The board shows ?. The website reports unknown, shows a dash instead of a distance and stops the warning. Do not move live sensor wires to force an error. If a safe test is not prepared, record Test not run and have the teacher arrange it.

Check loss of the connection. On Walking-stick sounds · tabletop model. A disconnected board must not leave an old warning sounding. Separately, more than three seconds without fresh complete messages makes the page show Signal paused. Click Disconnect and check that sound stops. Reconnect the same board and wait for a fresh result. Check. Disconnection clears the number and stops sound. Reconnecting shows a number only after a new usable reading. Signal paused also clears an old number. For a separate stale-stream check, the teacher can pause sending in a checked test copy while keeping Bluetooth connected. The labelled website demo’s Stop messages button tests the page timer only, not the sensor or Bluetooth.

Keep three real trials at each distance. In your existing team test record. One successful try can happen by chance. Repeat the same measured positions so failures are visible too. Run three trials at a ruler distance of 20 centimetres and three at 40 centimetres. For each, record ruler distance, website sensor distance, board display, website word and sound. Check. Six real trials show what happened, including any failed or missing readings. Keep ruler distance and sensor distance in separate columns. Write unavailable for a dash; never copy an old value or invent zero. Record differences as they happen.

Improve one thing and repeat the tests. In the same project and team test record. Changing one thing helps you see what caused a difference. Keep the original observations. If a correction is needed, make one teacher-checked correction using the first results. Download the next numbered .hex and copy it to MICROBIT. Wait for transfer, reconnect the sound page and repeat the same six trials. Check. If corrected, a separate after-change record can be compared with the original. If every trial worked, record that no correction was needed. Keep the original results and the 30 centimetres rule. If every trial worked, record that no correction was needed. If a correction is made, fix one thing, such as a wrong message branch or duplicate sender. Ask the teacher before changing physical settings or sensor timing.

Save the final program and results. In your existing team folder and shared report. The saved code should match the program that produced the recorded behavior. The guide itself does not collect answers. Keep the final numbered .hex and actual test notes in the team folder. Update Test and improvement in the shared report. Check. The next editor can find the working version, results and any untested behavior. Keep Project, Research, Test and improvement, References. Label missing tests honestly. Use the exact sources you actually consulted.

Use the existing team handoff. In Google Classroom · existing STEAM assignment. The teacher needs access to the shared report and the final program that your team demonstrates. This is the same project, not another assignment. Have one team member attach the shared report and final numbered .hex to the existing assignment by its announced deadline. Check. The files open for your teacher and match the demonstrated tabletop model. Each member explains their contribution and one actual result. The website does not submit files for you.
